Ezekiel Hopkins
ih-ZEE-kee-uhl HOP-kinz
proper noun (person)
English-born bishop and Puritan writer (1634-1690), Bishop of Derry in Ireland, author of expositions of the Ten Commandments and the Lord's Prayer.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Ezekiel Hopkins was an English-born preacher and bishop, eventually Bishop of Derry in Ireland, whose doctrinal sympathies were thoroughly Puritan and whose practical writings have outlived his episcopal office. His most enduring work is a full and searching Exposition of the Ten Commandments, which anatomizes the moral law with great spiritual penetration, showing the breadth of each commandment, the sins it forbids, and the duties it requires, and driving the convicted sinner to Christ. He wrote likewise on the Lord's Prayer, on the two covenants, on regeneration, and on the vanity of the world and glory of Christ. Hopkins held the law in the classic Reformed manner: it cannot justify, for no man keeps it, yet it remains the perfect rule of righteousness, exposing sin, restraining evil, and guiding the believer in the way of obedience. He stands in the dictionary as a master expositor of the moral law, who taught the church that the Ten Commandments are not abolished by grace but established by it, serving as a schoolmaster to bring sinners to Christ and a lamp to light the believer's grateful obedience.

EZEKIEL HOPKINS, proper noun. English-born preacher and Bishop of Derry (1634-1690).

Puritan in doctrine, practical in his enduring writings.

Author of a full Exposition of the Ten Commandments.

Wrote also on the Lord's Prayer, the two covenants, and regeneration.

Held the moral law as the perfect rule of righteousness that drives sinners to Christ.

📖 Key Scripture

Exo 20:3 — "Thou shalt have no other gods before me."

Matt 5:17 — "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."

Rom 7:12 — "Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good."

Gal 3:24 — "Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Hopkins's work guards against antinomianism, which discards the moral law altogether, and against legalism, which abuses it for justification; both errors miss the law's true Reformed uses.

expand to see more

Antinomian misreading. A common modern error treats the Ten Commandments as obsolete under grace, as though the gospel freed believers from the moral law itself. Hopkins, with the whole Reformed tradition, holds the opposite: Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it, and the believer, justified by faith, delights in the law as the rule of grateful obedience. The dictionary recovers the law's abiding place — it cannot save, but it is holy, just, and good, and grace writes it on the heart.

Legalist misreading. The opposite error abuses the law for self-justification, imagining that commandment-keeping earns God's favor. Hopkins exposes this too: the law's first work is to convict, to strip the sinner of self-righteousness and drive him to Christ as the schoolmaster drives the pupil. The dictionary holds the classic three uses of the law — to restrain, to convict, and to guide — against both the antinomian who discards it and the legalist who misuses it.
